title: Component Architecture at Scale
summary: How large frontend codebases stay maintainable across teams — feature-based structure, design systems as a product, monorepo tooling, and versioning a shared component library.

slides.markdown:
A ten-component app can be organized any way you like. A **five-hundred-component app touched by fifteen teams** cannot — without deliberate boundaries, every team's changes eventually collide with every other team's.

This topic covers the structural decisions that keep a large frontend codebase from calcifying: organizing by feature instead of by file type, treating a shared component library as a product with an API and a versioning story, and the monorepo-vs-polyrepo trade-off that decides how many teams can ship independently. The through-line is **dependency direction** — get it backwards once, and refactors that should take an hour take a quarter.

slides.sectionTitle: Structuring by feature, not by type
slides.markdown:
The naive structure groups files by *kind*: one folder of components, one of hooks, one of styles. It looks tidy at ten files and becomes unusable at a thousand — adding a feature means touching five unrelated folders, and deleting a feature means hunting for its scattered remains across all five.

**Feature-based structure** groups by *domain* instead: `features/checkout/` holds checkout's components, hooks, styles, and tests together. A shared, cross-feature layer (design-system components, generic utilities) sits alongside, not inside, any feature folder.

The practical payoff: a new engineer working on checkout only needs to open `features/checkout/`, and deleting a feature is deleting one directory. The cost is some duplication — two features might each have their own near-identical `useDebounce`, and that's an acceptable price for isolation until the duplication is proven, not assumed, to be worth centralizing.

slides.sectionTitle: A design system is a product, not a folder
slides.markdown:
A **design system** is the shared component library — buttons, inputs, modals, typography — that every feature team consumes instead of rebuilding. The mental shift that matters: treat it like a product with its own consumers (the feature teams), not like a `shared/` dumping ground that anyone can edit freehand.

That means it needs the things a product needs: a documented API (props, variants, accessibility guarantees), a changelog, an owning team that reviews changes, and a deprecation policy. Without ownership, a design system rots into exactly the disorganized `shared/` folder it was meant to replace — every consuming team bends it slightly for their own case until no shape is stable.

Companies at this scale (Shopify's Polaris, Atlassian's Design System, Google's Material) all treat their design system as a versioned, independently released package for exactly this reason.

slides.subTitle: App code, feature modules, design system
slides.markdown:
The rule that keeps a large codebase from becoming a tangle: **dependencies only point inward, never sideways or outward.** App shell code may depend on feature modules and the design system. Feature modules may depend on the design system. The design system depends on nothing feature-specific.

The violation to watch for is a design-system component importing something from a specific feature — a `Button` that knows about the checkout flow. Once that happens, the design system can no longer be released or tested independently, because it's silently coupled to one feature's release cadence.

slides.sectionTitle: Designing a component's API, not just its markup
slides.markdown:
A shared component's hardest design problem isn't its JSX — it's its **props API**, because that surface is what every future consumer is stuck with. Two patterns keep it from calcifying:

- **Composition over configuration.** A `Card` that accepts a `header`/`children`/`footer` slot composes with anything; a `Card` with `showHeader`, `headerTitle`, `headerIcon`, `headerAction` props grows a new flag for every consumer's variant.
- **Variant props over boolean soup.** A `variant="primary"|"danger"|"ghost"` prop scales cleanly to a tenth variant; five independent booleans (`isPrimary`, `isDanger`, `isGhost`...) produce combinations nobody intended and nobody tests.

The API is the contract the whole org depends on, so favor a slightly more verbose but composable shape over a terse one that only handles today's three consumers.

A **monorepo** holds multiple frontend apps and their shared packages (design system, utilities, types) in one repository with one dependency graph, versus a **polyrepo** where each app and library lives in its own repo, published and consumed as external packages.

The monorepo's core promise: a design-system change and every app that consumes it are visible in the same pull request, so a breaking change is caught by CI before it ships, not discovered by a downstream team weeks later. The cost is tooling — a naive setup rebuilds and retests everything on every change, so monorepos at scale need incremental build systems (Nx, Turborepo, Bazel) that only rebuild what actually changed, plus code ownership rules (`CODEOWNERS`) so one team's PR doesn't require review from every team in the repo.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: monorepo vs polyrepo for a multi-team org
slides.markdown:
| | Monorepo | Polyrepo |
|---|---|---|
| Cross-package changes | Atomic — one PR, CI catches breaks immediately | Split across repos — a breaking change ships silently until consumers update |
| Build/CI cost | Needs incremental tooling (Nx/Turborepo) or every change rebuilds everything | Each repo builds independently, naturally scoped |
| Team autonomy | Shared tooling/lint/CI config, harder to diverge | Each team picks its own tooling and release cadence |
| Onboarding | One clone, one set of docs | Must discover and clone N repos |
| Versioning story | Can use "always latest" internally, skip semver churn | Needs real semver + a publish step per change |

**How to decide:** a handful of tightly-coupled apps sharing a design system favors a monorepo; many loosely-coupled teams that genuinely want independent release cadence and tooling favor polyrepo, accepting slower cross-cutting changes as the price of autonomy.

slides.sectionTitle: Versioning a component library multiple teams consume
slides.markdown:
Once a design system has consumers outside the team that owns it, every change is a **backward-compatibility decision**. Semantic versioning gives the vocabulary: a patch (bug fix, no API change), a minor (new optional prop, additive), a major (a prop removed or its meaning changed, a visual change that breaks a consumer's assumption).

At real scale, a major version bump needs more than a changelog entry — teams ship **codemods** (automated find-and-replace scripts) alongside a breaking release so consumers can run one command to migrate instead of hand-editing every usage, and a deprecation window (old API still works, logs a warning, removed N releases later) instead of a hard cutover.

Skipping this ceremony is why some design systems get stuck on an old major version forever: the first breaking change with no migration path taught every consuming team to pin and never upgrade again.

slides.sectionTitle: What this looks like at real scale
slides.markdown:
Concrete numbers to anchor the discussion: a mature design system commonly ships **200–600 components and tokens**, is consumed by **dozens of internal apps**, and releases weekly or faster — which is exactly why it needs automated visual-regression testing (a pixel-diff on every component's stories) as a release gate, since no human reviews 600 components' rendering by eye before every release.

On the monorepo side, without incremental builds, a repo with 50 packages can see CI times climb past 20–30 minutes as it grows, which is the practical trigger for adopting a build-graph tool rather than a nice-to-have. Naming a number like this in an interview — "at that scale you need affected-only builds, not a full rebuild" — signals you've operated at this size, not just read about it.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: a "shared" component accumulating one-off props
slides.markdown:
**Wrong pattern:** team B needs the shared `Button` to look slightly different for one screen, so they add `isCompactForCheckoutV2`. Team C does the same for their case. A year later the component has 15 boolean props, most used by exactly one consumer, and nobody can tell which combinations are actually supported.

**Why it happens:** it's always locally faster to add one prop than to negotiate a general-purpose API with the owning team, so the incentive points the wrong way every single time.

**Correct model:** the owning team should push back on single-consumer props and instead offer composition primitives (slots, a `className`/`style` escape hatch, a render-prop) that let one team customize without adding a permanent flag to the shared surface. If a request keeps recurring across teams, that's the signal to add a real, documented variant — not a prop named after the team that asked for it.

Structure alone doesn't solve this — someone has to own the design system and the monorepo's shared tooling, or the discipline described in this topic erodes within a quarter. The staff-level nuance: this is an org-design problem as much as a code-design one.

Common models: a dedicated platform/design-systems team that reviews every change (strong consistency, can become a bottleneck at high change volume), or a **federated model** where any team can contribute via PR but the platform team owns final review and the versioning/release process (faster contribution, requires strong review discipline). Neither model works without `CODEOWNERS`-style enforcement — without it, "shared code owned by everyone" quietly becomes "shared code owned by no one," and the pitfall on the previous slide returns within a few sprints.
